issues.detail: Covers setup, TurboSnap and CI configuration well but gives little guidance on error scenarios such as build failures, missing or invalid tokens, flaky snapshots beyond determinism tips, or handling baseline conflicts across branches.
The workflow pins chromaui/action to @latest rather than a version tag or commit SHA, which is a minor supply-chain hygiene concern.
The CI example uses chromaui/action@latest, an unpinned third-party action, though it comes from the official vendor.

scenarios.name: multi-mode-button-snapshots
scenarios.rationale: Both define a shared modes file and apply it through parameters.chromatic.modes, and both note the theme global and snapshot cost. B states the rubric's theme-key caveat more precisely (it only has an effect if the preview defines a matching global, and light and dark render identically without it) and adds the stacking caveat. A is more thorough on setup but sets a default chromatic mode in preview.ts, and that default would stack with the component-level modes it later applies, which it never mentions.

scenarios.name: github-actions-chromatic-turbosnap
scenarios.rationale: Both include every rubric item (push trigger, fetch-depth 0, chromaui/action with the secret, onlyChanged, autoAcceptChanges: main, skip dependabot/**); B is a cleaner direct answer, while A adds a branches-ignore filter and a long preamble about not having written anything.

scenarios.name: stabilize-flaky-snapshots
scenarios.rationale: B directly uses parameters.chromatic ignoreSelectors and data-chromatic="ignore" for the price, disableSnapshot for the animated story, recommends deterministic data, and notes that a size change of an ignored element is still flagged. It also correctly says delay won't help with a looping animation, while A relies mostly on custom CSS and diffThreshold, never mentions disableSnapshot or ignoreSelectors, and never notes that a size change in an ignored element is still caught.
